questions.q: According to the professor, we postpone decisions mainly when:
options: The right course of action is not the one we want to take
questions.why: The travel enthusiast and the couch potato face the same holiday decision; only the want-vs-right gap differs.

questions.q: "Making a decision and executing it are two different things." The stalled step in the plant-head, delivery-head and product-manager examples is:
options: The execution, because preference conflicts with optimality
questions.why: In every case the numbers already point one way; the conflict with what they want to do is what defers action.

questions.q: The course of action is:
options: The alternative you choose, fully under your control
What the world does after you choose
questions.why: The farmer picks the crop; the monsoon is the state of nature.

questions.q: Buying TCS stock on Friday; the price moves on Monday. The Monday move is:
questions.why: Beyond your control after you choose.

questions.q: For a SOC, which pairing is correct?
options: Roster = course of action; alert volume = state of nature
Roster = state of nature; alert volume = course of action
questions.why: You choose the roster; the night's alerts and attackers are the world's move.

questions.q: The classification into certainty, risk and uncertainty is a statement about:
options: How much you know about the states of nature before you choose
questions.why: One outcome per action, known probabilities, or unknown probabilities.

questions.q: Decision making under certainty means:
options: Each course of action leads to exactly one known outcome
questions.why: Nothing is left to chance; the work is comparing known outcomes.

questions.q: In the FD example, the objective was fixed as:
options: Maximise the nominal maturity value of a one-year FD at a nationalised bank
Maximise real post-tax return across all instruments
questions.why: Change the objective and you change the whole decision problem - the objective function is sovereign.

questions.q: Why did the professor use Rs. 1 lakh and not Rs. 10 lakh in the FD example?
options: Tax rules change above Rs. 1 lakh
Deposit insurance covers up to Rs. 5 lakh per depositor per bank, so Rs. 1 lakh keeps the outcome certain even if the bank fails
Banks do not accept larger FDs
questions.why: Above Rs. 5 lakh a small probability of loss creeps in and the decision slides into risk.

questions.q: Planning delivery capacity against a signed multi-year contract book is decision making under:
options: None - it is not a decision
questions.why: The signatures pin down the states of nature; the new-business pipeline is what lives under risk.

questions.q: The tool for decisions under certainty is:
options: Comparison and optimisation - linear and integer programming
questions.why: Known outcomes, so the job is to optimise.

questions.q: The samosa-wala knows it rains about 3 days in 10 and that rain cuts sales to 80. His decision is under:
questions.why: Several states per action, with probabilities known from ten years of history.

questions.q: Frying 200 samosas at Rs. 5 cost and Rs. 10 price, with p(sunny) = 0.7 and rainy-day sales of 80, gives an EMV of:
EMV is the right criterion mainly for:
options: Repeated decisions, because it plays the long run
questions.why: For one-off decisions risk appetite matters too; the vendor is playing many days.

questions.q: March 2020 for most businesses was a decision environment of:
questions.why: The possible states were visible; nobody had probabilities for them.

questions.q: Jio launching free voice in 2016 is an example of:
options: Uncertainty - no precedent for how incumbents and customers would react
questions.why: A category-changing move with no historical data.

questions.q: Large plant: +100 / -40; small plant: +40 / +10 (Rs. lakh). The maximin criterion chooses:
questions.why: Best of the worst outcomes: small's +10 beats large's -40.

questions.q: With the same table, maximax chooses:
questions.why: Best of the best: 100 beats 40.

questions.q: With the same table, minimax regret chooses:
questions.why: If HIGH the regrets are 0 and 60; if LOW they are 50 and 0; large's worst regret (50) is the smaller.

questions.q: The Laplace criterion:
options: Treats the states as equally likely when there is no information
questions.why: Large: (100 - 40)/2 = 30 beats small: 25.

questions.q: The Hurwicz criterion:
options: Blends best and worst outcomes with an optimism index alpha between 0 and 1
questions.why: Alpha = 1 is maximax, alpha = 0 is maximin.

questions.q: The criteria disagreed (maximin said small, the rest said large). The professor's view of this is:
options: A sign the data is wrong
A reason to use EMV instead
An honest admission that under uncertainty the answer depends on temperament and the capacity to survive the worst case
questions.why: There are no probabilities to settle the argument.

questions.q: Frank Knight's distinction says:
options: Risk is measurable and can be priced (insured); uncertainty is unmeasurable and must be managed
questions.why: Insurance is a business precisely because risk is measurable.

questions.q: A zero-day exploit, as opposed to a known ransomware family, is a decision environment of:
questions.why: Known families come with frequency data; a zero-day comes with none.

questions.q: For any decision problem, the first step is to:
options: List the states of nature last
Classify the environment first - the tool follows the environment
questions.why: Write the objective, the courses of action, and what is known about the states of nature.

questions.q: A 99.9% availability SLA allows roughly how much downtime a year?
questions.why: 0.1% of 8,760 hours; scheduling maintenance inside it is integer programming.

questions.q: Integer programming is distinguished from linear programming by:
questions.why: A match happens in a slot or it does not; litres of a blend may be fractional.

questions.q: The IPL fixture was the professor's analogy for:
questions.why: Every team plays every other, grounds and broadcast slots have constraints, decisions are yes/no.

questions.q: Assigning 41 warehouses to cities once demand estimates are treated as known is:
options: A deterministic allocation problem solvable by optimisation
questions.why: Large, but certainty-world once demand is taken as known.

questions.q: The two decisions inside a Vehicle Routing Problem are:
options: Allocation of parcels to capacity-constrained vehicles, and sequencing of each route
questions.why: Which parcels go with whom, and in what order.

questions.q: A valid alternative objective for a VRP, mentioned in class, is:
questions.why: The choice of objective defines the problem.

questions.q: A PCB drilling machine visiting thousands of hole positions is:
options: A TSP hiding inside a factory
questions.why: One head, every hole once, minimum travel.

questions.q: The number of ways to sequence 10 stops is 10!, which equals about:
questions.why: 36,28,800; 15 stops is about 1.3 trillion.

questions.q: Checking every route for 20 stops at a billion routes a second would take about:
questions.why: 20! is about 2.43 x 10^18; 25 stops is about 490 million years.

questions.q: For a closed tour from a fixed depot, the number of distinct circular routes is:
options: (n - 1)!, halved again if direction does not matter
questions.why: The refinement barely matters - every version grows explosively.

questions.q: NP-hard means, in substance:
options: The problem is non-polynomial in name only
The problem cannot be solved at all
No known method guarantees the optimum quickly as size grows; brute force explodes
questions.why: The formally correct expansion is non-deterministic polynomial; the class shorthand was non-polynomial.

questions.q: Because routing is NP-hard, industry:
options: Uses heuristics that find a very good route in seconds rather than the perfect route in centuries
questions.why: Optimality sacrificed for tractability - a deep managerial lesson.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an NP-hard cousin mentioned in the notes?
questions.why: Comparing FD rates is a trivial comparison; the other three explode combinatorially.

questions.q: The shared file Detailed_Data.xls is the dataset of:
options: Pilgrim Bank (A): Customer Profitability, the HBS case by Frei and Campbell
questions.why: 31,634 US retail bank customers in 1999.

questions.q: The "9" prefix in the column names (9Profit, 9Online) means:
questions.why: The full file also has columns prefixed 0 for the year 2000.

questions.q: Mean profit is $111.50 and the median is $9. This tells you:
options: Profit is heavily skewed - a few very profitable customers pull the mean up
questions.why: The median tells the story the mean hides.

questions.q: 9Tenure is complete for every customer because:
options: It comes from the bank's own database - the customer did not have to supply it
questions.why: Age and income came from forms and are missing for about a quarter of customers.

questions.q: Roughly what share of Pilgrim customers were unprofitable in 1999?
questions.why: 14,580 of 31,634; the top 10% deliver about 70% of the profit.

questions.q: The four-step Pilgrim ladder for any "does X drive profit?" question is:
options: Compare group means; test significance; control for confounders; check missing-data bias
questions.why: Parts III and IV climb exactly this ladder.

questions.q: Sales data equals demand data:
options: Only until a stock-out; after that sales undercount demand and the data is censored
questions.why: The customers who found the shelf empty leave no trace; uncensoring estimates the demand you never saw.

questions.q: The Hawthorne effect warns that:
options: People behave differently when they know they are being watched, so pilot or audit data can flatter
questions.why: Size the plan on normal weeks, not the week the auditors were on the floor.

questions.q: In the Bass model, imitators are moved by:
options: Word of mouth - they adopt because others have (coefficient q)
questions.why: Innovators respond to external influence (p); imitators to internal influence (q); together they trace the S-curve.

questions.q: The Bass model is used when:
options: Five years of sales history exist
The product category does not yet exist, so there is no history to extrapolate
questions.why: Kindle, the first smartwatch - forecast adoption from the two kinds of buyers instead.

questions.q: The economic order quantity balances:
options: Ordering cost against holding cost - total cost is U-shaped and EOQ sits at its bottom
questions.why: Many small orders cost ordering effort; few large orders cost holding space and capital.

questions.q: Safety stock exists to:
options: Cover the uncertainty in demand and lead time that the EOQ formula cannot see
questions.why: The service version is surge capacity - extra analysts or riders for the night volume spikes.

questions.q: The bullwhip effect is best described as:
options: Small changes in consumer demand amplified up the supply chain - an information problem disguised as an inventory problem
questions.why: Independent forecasts, safety buffers, order batching, promotions and shortage gaming each add to the swing.

questions.q: CPFR fixes the bullwhip by:
options: Building one shared retailer-supplier forecast on shared point-of-sale data, with shorter order cycles
Holding more inventory at every tier
questions.why: Collaborative planning, forecasting and replenishment; vendor-managed inventory is a cousin.

questions.q: "With chaos comes revenue; with order comes profit" means:
options: Disruption creates the revenue opportunity; operational discipline is what turns it into profit
questions.why: Jio's launch created chaos and revenue; the profit needed operational order underneath.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the module's definition of a good decision?
options: One that follows the precedent that worked the last time
One that produces the desirable outcome
One approved by the most experienced person in the room
One based on logic, that considers all available data and alternatives and is arrived at through rational analysis
questions.why: Outcome, precedent and seniority are all substitutes for process; the definition is about the process and the information available at the time.

questions.q: "Being wrong feels exactly like being right." The point of this line was that:
options: Wrong decisions are as common as right ones
Emotions should be kept out of decision making
Until you discover you were wrong, your confidence is identical - so confidence is not evidence of being right
questions.why: Every feeling the class listed was the feeling of finding out; before that moment, wrong and right feel the same.

questions.q: Why does judging decisions by their outcome "promote mediocrity"?
options: It makes people take excessive risks to chase results
Outcomes are hard to measure accurately
People copy precedent as a safety net and avoid the full-potential option, because rewards and penalties follow outcomes
questions.why: When outcomes are rewarded and punished, everyone plays safe and the organisation settles in the middle - neither failing nor realising its potential.

questions.q: A manager used all available data and considered every option; the market turned bad and the product lost money. By the session's standard the decision was:
options: Good, because decision quality is judged on the process and the information available at the time
Bad, because the loss could have been predicted
questions.why: Under risk, a sound process can meet an unlucky state of nature; the outcome reflects chance, not the decision.

questions.q: In the Alcoa story, why was the plant executive fired?
options: An accident occurred on his plant
He tried to cover up an accident - the outcome mindset the CEO was eliminating
questions.why: Accidents were allowed to happen once; hiding one was not, because cover-ups mean the process is being fudged.

questions.q: Why could the unions not resist Paul O'Neill's changes to how work was done at Alcoa?
options: Every change was framed as removing a hazard to workers, which no union can oppose
He offered higher wages in return
questions.why: Safety was the door through which every process was re-examined; nobody can argue for keeping a hazardous process.

questions.q: The stock price fell immediately after O'Neill's first speech. This illustrates:
options: The market grading a leader on an early "outcome" before any process had been built
That safety programmes destroy shareholder value
questions.why: The analysts judged the outcome of one speech; the process he built took thirteen years to show in profits.

questions.q: Why does design thinking forbid talking about solutions in its first steps?
options: Problems are more interesting than solutions
Once invested in a solution, we reshape the problem so that the solution fits it
questions.why: Emotional investment in a solution creates the bias of moulding the problem to fit; the ban protects step one.

questions.q: For the blind child who wants to play basketball, the session's "real problem" was:
options: The child cannot independently navigate an unfamiliar space
Basketball is unsafe for the child
questions.why: "Cannot see" is the symptom; the navigation problem is the one echolocation actually solves.

questions.q: Which is the professor's test that you treated a symptom rather than the root cause?
options: The fix cost more than the budget
The next fire arrives without a significant period of calm
The team disagreed with the fix
The fix took longer than a week
questions.why: Calm after a fix is the evidence that the cause was treated; back-to-back fires mean the cause is still there.

questions.q: If firefighting happens daily, which of these was NOT listed as a possible reason?
options: The team is not aligned or motivated
The processes are fine but their implementation is broken
The organisation has too many strategic projects
questions.why: The four listed reasons were broken processes, broken implementation, an unaligned team, and treating symptoms - not too much strategy.

questions.q: Which step of the six-step process should receive the most time?
questions.why: "Solving the right problem roughly beats solving the wrong problem accurately" - steps 5 and 6 are mechanical.

questions.q: Which of these is a state of nature rather than a course of action?
options: Charging a fee for online banking
questions.why: The other three are choices under the decision-maker's control; the market's reaction is not.

questions.q: "What is the probability that TLC chooses the large plant?" The correct response is:
options: One in three, since there are three alternatives
It equals the EMV divided by the payoff
The question is malformed - alternatives are chosen (1 or 0); only states of nature carry probabilities
questions.why: The professor stressed this point: you pick alternatives, you do not roll dice on them.

questions.q: Why does the six-step process insist on listing ALL alternatives?
options: To make the payoff table larger
To neutralise the bias that quietly drops options we dislike or over-favours our own idea before the analysis begins
Because the model cannot run with fewer than three
questions.why: The rival's-product example: national launch vanishes from a rival's list, the small-town test vanishes from your own.

questions.q: A payoff in step 4 need NOT be:
options: Tied to the performance measure of the decision
questions.why: Market share is a perfectly valid payoff; "monetary" in EMV is only a label.

questions.q: Decision making under uncertainty differs from decision making under risk in that:
options: Under risk the outcome of each action is certain
Uncertainty uses EMV while risk uses linear programming
Under uncertainty there is only one state of nature
Under uncertainty the probabilities of the states are unknown; under risk they are estimated
questions.why: Both have several states of nature; the difference is whether you can attach probabilities.

questions.q: Amazon launching the Kindle before e-readers existed as a category is an example of decision making under:
questions.why: No historical data and no probability estimates for how the market would react - "shooting in the dark".

questions.q: Tools for decision making under certainty include:
questions.why: Under certainty each action has one known outcome, so the job is optimisation - operations research.

questions.q: Per the session, using gut feeling in analytical decision making is:
options: Acceptable, because it is inference from a sample of experience - what is unacceptable is stubbornness when the evidence disagrees
Only acceptable for the most senior person
questions.why: Gut feeling works like statistics - a sample generalised to the whole; the sin is refusing to examine it.

questions.q: The Challenger engineers' chart failed to convince because:
options: It showed only launches with O-ring problems, omitting the successful launches that all sat at warmer temperatures
It had too few data points to plot
It was drawn by managers rather than engineers
It used the wrong temperature units
questions.why: Failures alone appeared at all temperatures; adding the successes showed that no clean launch had happened below the threshold.

questions.q: The lesson the professor drew from Challenger was:
options: Launch schedules should never be delayed
Gut feeling should be ignored in engineering
The engineers' gut was right but they never found the data to support it - look at the successes, not only the failures
questions.why: Their instinct was correct and later proved; what failed was the second check - finding the right data.

questions.q: The EMV of an alternative is:
options: Its payoff minus its opportunity loss
The probability-weighted average of its payoffs across the states of nature
questions.why: A weighted average where the weights are the probabilities - the professor's translation for non-mathematicians.

questions.q: At P = 0.5, EMV of the large plant is:
The EMV criterion selects the SMALLEST EMV when:
options: The payoff is a cost or risk measure, where smaller is better
There are more than two states of nature
Never - it always selects the largest
questions.why: "Best" depends on the payoff: largest for profit, revenue or share; smallest for cost, risk or defects.

questions.q: "The small plant never actually earns 40,000." The right interpretation of EMV = 40,000 is:
options: It is a rounding artefact of the table
It is the long-run average per instance if the same decision were repeated many times under the same probabilities
questions.why: Over ten launches, five favourable and five unfavourable, the small plant nets 400,000 - 40,000 per launch.

questions.q: Over ten repetitions with five favourable and five unfavourable markets, the large plant nets in total:
EOL minimisation compared with EMV maximisation:
questions.why: The mathematics guarantees the same choice; that is why the class focuses on EMV.

questions.q: For TLC at P = 0.5, the EOL of the small plant is:
questions.why: Regrets are 100,000 (favourable) and 20,000 (unfavourable): 0.5 x 100,000 + 0.5 x 20,000 = 60,000 - which also equals EVPI.

questions.q: The range of P (probability of a favourable market) over which the small plant is the best choice is:
questions.why: Below 0.167 do nothing wins; above 0.615 the large plant wins; the small plant holds the middle.

questions.q: If P = 0.70, EMV recommends:
If P = 0.60, EMV recommends:
questions.why: 0.60 is still below the 0.615 threshold: small = 52,000 beats large = 48,000. The 0.5 estimate is irrelevant; the threshold is what matters.

questions.q: A decision is called "sensitive" when:
options: A small change in an input flips the recommended alternative
The payoff table has more than three rows
questions.why: Sensitivity analysis asks how much the inputs can move before the answer changes; a thin cushion means sensitive.

questions.q: When sensitivity analysis shows a very thin cushion, the professor's advice is to:
options: Buy perfect information at any price
Proceed, but prepare a contingency plan - accepting that risk management has a cost
Choose the alternative with the smallest possible loss instead
Abandon the decision until better data arrives
questions.why: If the upper threshold were 0.515 nobody's gut can tell 50% from 51%; so line up suppliers, a leased plant or a subcontractor in advance.

questions.q: EVPI equals:
options: The cost of a market survey
The best payoff in the table
The EMV of the best alternative
The expected value with perfect information minus the best EMV without it
questions.why: Worth of information = what you make with it minus what you make without it.

questions.q: EVwPI for TLC is 100,000 because:
options: It is the sum of the positive payoffs divided by three
It is the large-plant payoff halved
It is the best payoff in each state weighted by that state's probability: 0.5 x 200,000 + 0.5 x 0
questions.why: Take the best payoff in each state and weight it by that state’s probability: 0.5 × 200,000 + 0.5 × 0 = 100,000.

questions.q: Information is worth paying for only if:
options: Its cost is below the best payoff
It comes from a reputed agency
It would change the course of action you would otherwise take
questions.why: If you would do the same thing with or without it, it is worth nothing however accurate it is.

questions.q: A consultant offers TLC perfect information about the market for Rs. 65,000. TLC should:
options: Accept only if the probability of a favourable market is 0.5
Decline, since EVPI of 60,000 is the ceiling on what the information is worth
Accept, since 65,000 exceeds the small plant's EMV
questions.why: Any price above 60,000 leaves TLC worse off than deciding without the information.

questions.q: In computing EVwPI, the informant's "favourable" and "unfavourable" messages are weighted 0.5 and 0.5 because:
options: EMV happened to be computed at 0.5
Perfect information is always a 50-50 proposition
They are our own estimates of the market, and we cannot hold two different estimates of the same thing
The informant has exactly two possible messages
questions.why: Had the prior been 60-40, a truthful informant would say "favourable" 60 percent of the time.

questions.q: The Calcutta bakery could reduce its demand uncertainty most directly by:
options: Discarding fewer items at closing time
Offering a pre-booking discount funded from EVPI, converting some walk-ins into committed orders
questions.why: The customer is the one who can remove tomorrow's demand uncertainty, and needs an incentive to do so; EVPI caps that incentive.

questions.q: Per the session, OnePlus's invite-only launch and Xiaomi's flash sales were:
options: Marketing tactics creating scarcity and exclusivity - not uncertainty-management devices
Ways to obtain perfect demand information
questions.why: They created the feeling of owning something not everyone can get; inventory was not the constraint.

questions.q: In a decision tree:
options: Squares are chance nodes and circles are decision nodes
Both node types are drawn from right to left
Branches out of a square carry probabilities
Squares are decision nodes whose branches are courses of action; circles are outcome nodes whose branches are states of nature with probabilities
questions.why: Square = you choose; circle = nature decides. Only the circle's branches have probabilities.

questions.q: A decision tree is drawn from left to right in the sequence in which events unfold so that:
options: It fits on a landscape slide
You never assume information that will not yet be available, and you see what you will know at each point
questions.why: The sequence is the discipline: read the survey before you choose the plant, not after.

questions.q: Solving ("folding back") a decision tree means:
options: Working right to left: computing expected value at circles, choosing the best branch at squares and marking the rejected ones
Working right to left, choosing the best branch at circles
Working left to right, computing EMV at squares
questions.why: Branches fold into their nearest node: average at circles, choose at squares, slash what you drop.

questions.q: In the survey tree, what immediately follows the "conduct survey" branch?
options: A decision node with large, small and no plant
A chance node for the survey result - favourable (0.45) or unfavourable (0.55) - because you read the report before deciding
questions.why: Drawing a square straight after the survey was the mistake most of the class made.

questions.q: Why do the payoffs on the survey side read 190,000 and -190,000 instead of 200,000 and -180,000?
options: The Rs. 10,000 survey cost is committed the moment you decide to survey, so every payoff on that side is reduced by 10,000
Because of a five percent tax
Because the probabilities changed to 0.78 and 0.22
questions.why: Even "no plant" becomes -10,000 on the survey side; the money is spent regardless of what follows.

questions.q: Given a favourable survey result, the best action and its EMV are:
Given an unfavourable survey result, the best action and its EMV are:
The EMV of "conduct the survey" (node 1) is:
EVSI for the TLC survey is:
questions.why: Value with the survey if it were free (49,200 + 10,000 = 59,200) minus 40,000 without it; 9,200 is the net gain after paying.

questions.q: TLC's optimal strategy is:
options: Survey; build large if favourable, nothing if unfavourable
Survey; build large if favourable, small if unfavourable
Survey; build small in both cases
Skip the survey and build the small plant
questions.why: The folded-back tree prescribes a complete policy, not a single action - that is what a table cannot do.

questions.q: Which of the following is always true?
options: EVSI is greater than or equal to EVPI
EVSI is zero whenever the survey costs money
EVSI equals EVPI minus the survey cost
EVSI is less than or equal to EVPI
questions.why: Imperfect information can never be worth more than perfect information: 19,200 against 60,000 here.

questions.q: P(favourable market | survey favourable) = 0.78 and P(unfavourable market | survey unfavourable) = 0.73 are not symmetric because:
options: A test's false-positive and false-negative error rates need not be equal - as with the COVID rapid antigen test
questions.why: Different error rates, and different stakes for each error, are the norm rather than the exception.

questions.q: Why should a survey vendor's historical accuracy (say 70 percent) NOT be plugged straight into the tree?
options: The probabilities must be customised to the current prior - a near-certain product and a 50-50 product cannot get identical survey probabilities
questions.why: The COVID-vaccine example: a survey on a 90-10 product must point more confidently than the same survey on a coin toss.

questions.q: With a prior of 0.5/0.5, P(survey positive | favourable) = 0.70 and P(survey positive | unfavourable) = 0.20, the posterior P(favourable | survey positive) is:
questions.why: Joint probabilities 0.35 and 0.10 sum to 0.45; 0.35 / 0.45 = 0.78.

questions.q: P(survey positive) = 0.45 was obtained as:
questions.why: The total of the joint probabilities across both states of nature - the denominator in Bayes' theorem.

questions.q: The Pilgrim Bank assignment asks whether to charge a fee or offer a rebate for online banking. The rebate makes sense when:
options: Online banking lowers the bank's servicing cost, so migrating customers online is worth paying for
questions.why: The fee logic applies when online banking is an additional facility on top of continued branch cost.

questions.q: Sales data equals demand data only when:
questions.why: After a stock-out, sales undercount demand - the campus-session point the class recalled.

questions.q: Ross selling last season's bag at a permanently lower price is:
options: A markdown - a permanent reduction once demand falls short
An event discount like Zara on Black Friday
questions.why: A true markdown never returns to the original price; Zara's Black Friday price does.

questions.q: The professor's distinction between a fishbone diagram and a decision tree is:
options: Fishbone is for root-cause analysis (chains of why); the tree structures the solution once the problem is defined
Both solve the same problem in different notation
The tree is for root cause; the fishbone for options
Fishbone is for numbers; the tree is for pros and cons
questions.why: Fishbone belongs before step one; the tree belongs after step four.

questions.q: The CPWD architect's Canada decision illustrates:
options: A well-informed decision with a poor outcome (COVID) still being a good decision - process over outcome
That personal decisions cannot use trees
questions.why: The tree in his diary showed he had let go of what he had chosen to let go of; COVID was not knowable.

questions.q: The slide's five steps of decision tree analysis are:
options: Define the problem; draw the tree; assign probabilities to the states of nature; estimate payoffs; solve by computing EMVs at the state-of-nature nodes
List alternatives; compute EOL; buy information; survey; launch
questions.why: Steps 3 and 4 put numbers on the tree; step 5 folds it back from the right.

questions.q: Decision trees are most beneficial when:
options: A sequence of decisions must be made, such as survey first and then choose the plant
The payoff table has two columns
questions.why: Any decision table can be drawn as a tree; a sequence of decisions cannot be held in a table at all.

questions.q: According to the slide, probability values for a tree can come from:
options: Management's experience and intuition, historical data, or computation from other data using Bayes' theorem
questions.why: Bayes incorporates the initial estimate and the accuracy of the information source, and revises the estimate as new information arrives.

questions.q: EVwPI is defined as:
options: The long-run average return if perfect information were available before each decision: the best payoff in each state, weighted by that state's probability
The best single payoff in the table
The EMV of the best alternative

questions.q: Google testing a new product first inside the team, then with family and friends, then with all employees, then in a beta is an example of:
options: Converting uncertainty into risk with proxies - each stage produces an estimate you can put on a tree
questions.why: Most decisions start in uncertainty; proxies move them into the risk column.

questions.q: The kirana store owner facing a new dark store two streets away lists: start own delivery, list on a platform, or do nothing. Those three are:
questions.why: How heavily the neighbourhood takes to delivery is the state of nature; monthly profit is the payoff.

sections.name: Session 3: From data to an estimate

questions.q: When a student said the Pilgrim data was too messy and incomplete to support a decision, the professor's response was that:
options: Real business data is always messy, and not deciding is usually not one of the options
Only the rows with complete age and income should be used
More data should be collected before deciding
The decision should wait for the year-2000 columns
questions.why: Missing values are the normal condition of data; postponing a decision usually means it gets taken for you when options expire.

questions.q: Making every survey question mandatory tends to:
options: Make people abandon the survey or type garbage
Eliminate missing values with no side effects
Improve the quality of the answers
questions.why: The information you want is not the respondent's obligation; forcing it produces exits or junk.

questions.q: In the professor's framing, retaining customers and building relationships are:
options: Means to an end that comes from the vision, mission and strategy
The end goal of every for-profit company
questions.why: Retention is a means; the end is profit for a for-profit firm (or market share for a start-up in its valuation phase).

questions.q: Loyalty bought with freebies is weak because:
options: Only large companies can afford them
Customers seek value, and someone who came for a freebie leaves for the next one
questions.why: Solid loyalty comes from value delivered over a long time, not from a rebate.

questions.q: On the profitability skew (Exhibit 3), the horizontal axis is:
options: Cumulative % of customers, sorted from most to least profitable
questions.why: Sorting descending by profit is what makes "the top 10%" mean the ten percent most profitable customers.

questions.q: The top 10% most profitable customers bring roughly what share of the year's profit?
questions.why: The computed figure is 69.2%; 97% is the top 20% and 121% is the peak at about 53%.

questions.q: The top 20% most profitable customers bring roughly:
questions.why: 97.1% - which the class rounded to "about 100%". 80% is the classic Pareto figure, not this bank's.

questions.q: The curve rises above 100% because:
options: The cumulative profit of the profitable customers exceeds the net total, and the loss-makers then pull it back down
questions.why: At the peak every profitable customer has been added ($4.29 million) and no loss-maker yet.

questions.q: The peak of the curve occurs at:
options: The last customer with a positive profit, about 53% of customers
questions.why: Customer 16,832 is the last one with profit above zero; everyone after subtracts.

questions.q: The professor read the 121.6% peak as:
options: Letting go of roughly the bottom half of customers would have raised last year's profit by about 20%
The bank overstated its profit by 21.6%
questions.why: The loss-making tail returned 21.6 points of the profit the good customers had earned.

questions.q: How many customers in the file were loss-making in 1999?
questions.why: 14,580 customers (46.1%) had negative profit; 16,832 were profitable; 3,854 and 27,780 are the online and offline counts.

questions.q: In the recipe =A2/$E$1 for the percentage of customers, the dollar signs are there to:
options: Keep the total-customers cell fixed when the formula is dragged down
Convert the result to a percentage
questions.why: Without the absolute reference, dragging would move the denominator down a row each time.

questions.q: The chart type the professor used for the skew, and why:
options: Pie chart, because the shares add to 100%
Scatter with markers only, because lines through 31,634 points make a cluttered mess
Stacked bar, to show losses separately
Line chart, because the points are ordered
questions.why: Markers only; and tidy the axes to 20%, 40% ... rather than 0.2000 for the reader's sake.

questions.q: Can a bank explicitly refuse to serve a customer because they were loss-making last year?
options: Generally no - in India it cannot refuse service and in the West it would be treated as discrimination - so it uses implicit means
questions.why: Refusal risks the licence; preferential treatment achieves the same end quietly.

questions.q: The professor's 27-minute JetPrivilege wait, against her husband's one-minute connection, illustrates:
options: Deliberate steering of low-tier customers to cheap channels so agents stay free for high-tier customers
questions.why: The queue did not vanish when she hung up; Gold and Silver tiers are routed ahead of Blue.

questions.q: A Rs. 10,000 annual card fee that is waived above a spending threshold is designed to:
options: Keep undesirable customers out while the profitable ones never pay it
questions.why: One rule for everyone, two effects: the fee filters entrants, the waiver retains the profitable.

questions.q: In Subarna's bank, a customer who stops meeting the profitability score for a tier is:
options: Downgraded to the next tier, where the cost to serve and the facilities are both lower
questions.why: Graduated, not abrupt: the customer is weaned off expensive service rather than fired.

questions.q: Gopal's car insurer refusing to renew after two claims above Rs. 1 lakh is an example of:
options: Explicit refusal - possible in insurance, unthinkable for a bank account
questions.why: The professor added that many organisations do this through faulty systems rather than deliberate policy.

questions.q: The Pareto principle says:
options: A small share of the causes or elements accounts for most of the effect
20% of the profit comes from 80% of customers
questions.why: The exact split varies (this bank is nearer 20/97); the shape and the management response are the same.

questions.q: In total quality management, the Pareto idea implies that:
options: A handful of root causes produce most of the defects, so fix those first
questions.why: Fix the vital few causes and most of the symptoms disappear with them.

questions.q: In this data, the top 20% of customers bring what share of the profit earned by the profitable customers (before losses are netted)?
questions.why: $3,423,486 of $4,288,303 is 79.8% - the 80/20 rule almost exactly; 97% is the share of the net total.

questions.q: Koutons' "50% + 40% off" is a total discount of:
questions.why: The 40% comes off the remaining half: 50% + 40% of 50% = 70%. Cantabil's 50% + 49% is about 75%.

questions.q: A full-price retailer that is on sale most days of the year is showing:
options: Poorly managed demand - stock that did not sell has to be marked down
Price jacking, as the professor's grandmother believed
questions.why: Koutons discounts by design; Shoppers Stop or Marks and Spencer discount because forecasting and lead times failed them.

questions.q: "Remember, you are buying to sell, not to wear yourself" warns merchandisers against:
options: Substituting their own taste for the target customer's
questions.why: Consolidation put buying in the hands of people who are not the customer - a NIFT graduate buying for a value store.

questions.q: Offshoring apparel manufacturing to China, Vietnam and Bangladesh worsened discounting because:
options: Long lead times and logistics costs stop retailers responding to trends, so the wrong stock piles up
questions.why: Orders go in months ahead; your size sells out while the unwanted shades wait for the sale.

questions.q: Zara replenishes its stores roughly every:
questions.why: Frequent replenishment from centralised production, small displays and city fulfilment centres are all aligned around fast fashion.

questions.q: Delayed differentiation means:
options: Keeping generic components or a base product and customising at the last step, as Dell and Asian Paints do
Postponing markdowns to the end of the season
Cutting the number of brands stocked
questions.why: Stock components, not finished variety: the same component serves many configurations; pigments are mixed to order.

questions.q: Where can variety NOT easily be reduced, according to the class?
options: A value supermarket with strong bargaining power
A departmental store - drop the item a customer came for and they take all their shopping elsewhere
questions.why: Padmanabhan's example; Dell, Asian Paints and DMart were the cases where it works.

questions.q: The lesson of Spencer's late and struggling Jiffy quick-delivery service is that:
options: Online channels should not be launched after COVID
Quick commerce cannot work for supermarkets
Starting a new channel is easy; aligning every process behind it is where businesses fail
questions.why: Many post-COVID online channels died for the same reason.

questions.q: A population is best defined as:
options: The sample plus the people who did not respond
The set of all elements that are of interest to the study
questions.why: Both halves matter: all the elements, and only those this study cares about - so it changes from study to study.

questions.q: For an inventory-management study, the "elements" of the population would be:
questions.why: For a defects study they would be the possible root causes; for Pilgrim they are customers.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the reasons the professor gave for using a sample instead of the population?
options: It is sometimes impossible, as in destructive testing
A sample is more accurate than population data
questions.why: The population is always better if you can afford it in money and time; a sample is the fallback.

questions.q: Which is an example of destructive testing?
options: Lighting an LED bulb and leaving it on until it fails, noting the hours
questions.why: The measured unit cannot be sold afterwards, so testing the whole population would leave nothing to sell.

questions.q: Honda's decision not to give the 2001 Activa a spare wheel was:
options: A talking point backed by a tyre-life claim that could only come from testing a sample destructively
questions.why: Priced like a bike, shaped like a scooter, no stepney - and a claim of about 5,000 trouble-free kilometres.

questions.q: A sample is representative of the population when:
options: It was chosen by a method that gave every element an equal chance of inclusion
It is at least 10% of the population
It has the same demographic mix as the population
questions.why: The definition is about the method, not the mix - you cannot balance on infinitely many characteristics.

questions.q: A population of 5,000 men and 5,000 women; a sample of 100. Must it contain 50 men and 50 women?
options: Only if the question is one where men and women are likely to answer differently
Only if the sample is smaller than 30
questions.why: Balance for a trait only when it drives the answer; otherwise forcing the balance introduces bias.

questions.q: In stratified sampling, the strata in the sample should be in:
options: The same ratio as in the population, e.g. 60/40 if the population is 60/40
questions.why: And within each stratum the elements are drawn by simple random sampling.

questions.q: Within each stratum of a stratified sample, elements are chosen by:
options: Taking the first names on the list
questions.why: Stratification fixes the ratio; randomness inside each stratum keeps the sample fair.

questions.q: The main danger of convenience sampling is:
options: Bias - the people who responded may differ systematically from those who did not
questions.why: You did not choose the sample; the respondents did.

questions.q: A school reports that its alumni earn Rs. 75 lakh a year on average, based on replies to a reunion survey. The most likely problem is:
options: Non-response bias: those doing badly stayed silent while a few unicorn founders replied
questions.why: A segment of the population was far more likely to respond and dragged the average up.

questions.q: Rare-event sampling is needed when:
options: The phenomenon is so rare that a random draw would never find the cases
The data is a time series
questions.why: A one-in-a-million disease will not appear in a simple random sample; most managers never need this method.

questions.q: Statistically, a "large sample" is one with:
options: At least 30 elements, regardless of the population size
questions.why: An absolute number, not a percentage - the class's 10% answer was the corporate convention, not the statistics.

questions.q: The reason 30 is the threshold is:
options: The central limit theorem: sample averages start to follow the bell curve once samples have about 30 or more elements
questions.why: That regularity is what the estimation and testing formulas rely on.

questions.q: Beyond 30, a larger sample buys you:
options: Precision - a smaller cushion around every estimate
questions.why: Permission arrives at 30; accuracy keeps improving with the square root of n.

questions.q: The three things a sample is used for are:
options: Simple random, stratified and convenience sampling
Estimation, hypothesis testing and identifying relationships (regression)
questions.why: This session did estimation; Session 4 does hypothesis testing; regression comes later.

questions.q: An exit poll is an example of:
questions.why: Nobody asks every voter; a sample estimates the share in favour.

questions.q: The fine print "tested on 1,000 subjects under laboratory conditions" exists because:
options: A claim like "lasts 3,000 hours" or "makes you taller" must rest on sample evidence that can be defended in a hypothesis test
It is a legal formality with no statistical content
questions.why: Syska, Horlicks and hair-fall shampoos have all been challenged by consumer groups; the sample is the defence.

questions.q: Working out how much pre-launch promotion to spend to hit a first-quarter sales target is:
options: Regression - identifying the relationship and solving backwards
questions.why: If sales are a known function of promotion, a Rs. 50 crore target can be turned into a promotion budget.

questions.q: The Pilgrim 1999 file is:
options: Cross-sectional data - many customers at one point in time
questions.why: It is a snapshot; following the same customers into 2000 and 2001 would make it a panel.

questions.q: India's GDP from 1991 to 2025 is:
questions.why: One variable, many points in time; the 2025 GDP of 200 countries would be cross-sectional.

questions.q: Panel data is:
options: Many elements, each followed over time - the most powerful of the three
Data from a consumer panel survey
Many elements at one point in time
questions.why: For each country a time series, for each year a cross-section, and the whole picture together.

questions.q: Why did the case use cross-sectional data as a proxy instead of an experiment with a control group?
options: Tracking two groups for five to ten years is too slow - the technology would be obsolete by then
Control groups need more than 30 customers
questions.why: So the question becomes "are online customers more profitable than offline customers?" rather than "does going online make a customer more profitable?".

questions.q: A population parameter, such as the true average profit of all five million customers, is:
questions.why: If we had every row we would all compute the same number; we just do not have every row.

questions.q: A sample mean is a random variable because:
options: Its value depends on who happens to land in the sample
questions.why: Sample the batch's work experience from the three most senior people and the mean is high; from the three youngest and it is low.

questions.q: The deviations of the values from their mean always:
questions.why: The mean is the centre of gravity of the data, so negatives and positives cancel - hence the squaring.

questions.q: The difference between STDEV.S and STDEV.P in Excel is that:
options: S divides by n; P divides by n - 1
S divides the sum of squares by n - 1; P divides by n
S is for small samples only
questions.why: S for sample (31,633), P for population (31,634); negligible here, material with a handful of values.

questions.q: Why n - 1 for a sample variance?
options: Because the sample mean has already used up one degree of freedom, and dividing by n - 1 makes the estimate unbiased
questions.why: Given the mean and nine of ten values, the tenth is determined - only nine are free to vary.

questions.q: For the sample 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, the sample variance is:
questions.why: Sum of squares 10, divided by n - 1 = 4. Dividing by 5 gives the population variance 2.0; 1.58 is the SD.

questions.q: The standard deviation is expressed in:
options: The same units as the data
questions.why: Variance is in squared units; the square root brings it back - $272.84 is in dollars.

questions.q: Whether a standard deviation is "large" is judged:
options: Relative to the mean - $273 is trivial against a $50,000 mean and enormous against $111.50
questions.why: Then check mean +/- 1 SD and ask whether that range could support the decision.

questions.q: For a normal distribution, mean +/- 1 SD contains about:
Mean +/- 1 SD for the Pilgrim profit data is:
questions.why: 111.50 +/- 272.84. The first option is what the range would be if the SD were 20; the third is the offline confidence interval.

questions.q: If the mean were $111.50 but the SD were $20, mean +/- 1 SD would be:
questions.why: Now you could say the average customer is profitable, and by roughly how much - the point of the comparison.

questions.q: The median profit is $9 while the mean is $111.50. This indicates:
options: That the SD must be small
A distribution skewed by a tail of very profitable customers
questions.why: Half the customers earn the bank $9 or less; a few earn up to $2,071 and pull the mean up.

questions.q: The offline customers' mean profit and standard deviation are:
questions.why: The second pair is online; the third is everyone; the fourth is the offline confidence interval.

questions.q: The number of online customers in the file is:
questions.why: 27,780 are offline; 3,142 is the count for district 1100.

questions.q: A student proposed dropping the loss-making customers before comparing online and offline. The professor said:
options: Only drop customers with missing age
No - those customers stay in the population the fee or rebate will apply to, and rules must be identical for everyone
questions.why: A threshold rule (fee waived above Rs. 3 lakh of spend) is legitimate because it is the same rule for all.

questions.q: A rebate can be worth paying even when:
options: The customer never uses online banking
It only reduces a customer's loss, say from $50 offline to $30 online
Online customers are less profitable in every group
questions.why: Reducing losses counts; a rebate does not have to make everyone profitable.

questions.q: Why could the class not conclude that online customers are more profitable from $116.67 versus $110.79?
options: The online sample is too large
The gap is under 6% while the SDs are around $270-280, so a different sample could easily reverse it
Age was missing for some customers
questions.why: Sample means are random variables; with that much spread the population could be the other way round.

questions.q: A point estimate is:
options: A range with an upper and lower limit
A single number offered as the best guess of a population parameter
questions.why: The sample mean of $111.50 is the point estimate of the population mean.

questions.q: At "gunpoint", everyone in the class gave a range for the pen's price because:
options: A range has a far higher chance of being right than a single number
questions.why: High stakes make you demand accuracy, and you buy accuracy by widening the range.

questions.q: Minus infinity to plus infinity is a 100% confidence interval. It is:
options: Certainly right and completely useless - which is why 100% confidence is never used
questions.why: Confidence and usefulness trade off; 90%, 95% and 99% are the working compromises.

questions.q: A confidence interval is built as:
options: Mean plus or minus one standard deviation
Median plus or minus the SD
Minimum to maximum of the sample
Point estimate plus or minus a cushion
questions.why: The cushion is z times the SD divided by the square root of n; mean +/- 1 SD describes the data, not the estimate.

questions.q: You should choose 99% rather than 90% confidence when:
options: The cost of going wrong is very high
questions.why: The level is a business choice driven by the cost of error; higher confidence costs you a wider interval.

questions.q: The multiplier z for a 95% confidence interval is:
The multiplier z for a 99% confidence interval is:
questions.why: Wider than 95%: more confidence means a bigger cushion.

questions.q: The cushion of a confidence interval grows with:
options: The confidence level and the SD, and shrinks with the sample size
questions.why: z and sigma sit on top of the formula; the square root of n sits underneath.

questions.q: Doubling the sample size reduces the cushion by:
options: A factor of the square root of 2, about 29%
questions.why: The square root is why you need four times the data to halve the cushion.

questions.q: The 95% confidence interval for offline customers' average profit is:
questions.why: The second is online; the third is all customers; the fourth is mean +/- 1 SD.

questions.q: The online interval ($17.9 wide) is about three times the offline interval ($6.4) mainly because:
options: The online SD is much higher
The online sample is far smaller (3,854 against 27,780), and n sits in the denominator
questions.why: The SDs are similar ($284 against $271); the sample size does almost all the work.

questions.q: The correct way to state the offline result is:
options: Offline profit will be $113.98 next year
95% of offline customers earn between $107.60 and $113.98
With 95% confidence, the population average profit from an offline customer lies between $107.60 and $113.98
The average offline customer earns exactly $110.79
questions.why: The interval is about the population mean, not about individual customers.

questions.q: The two 95% intervals overlap between $107.7 and $114.0. Therefore:
options: Online is more profitable because its upper limit is higher
Offline is more profitable because its interval is tighter
Nothing can be concluded - the true means could sit either way round
The two groups are equally profitable
questions.why: Case A (offline 113.5, online 108.5) and Case B (offline 108, online 124) are both consistent with the data.

questions.q: "Online must be more profitable - its interval goes up to $125.6." This reasoning is wrong because:
options: The online sample is too small to count
The true value can be anywhere in its interval, not preferentially near the upper end
questions.why: The professor called this the most common mistake made with confidence intervals.

questions.q: Non-overlapping intervals would allow a conclusion even if:
options: Only if the SDs were equal
Never - overlap is not the test
Only if the sample sizes were equal
questions.why: What matters is overlap, not matching sizes; new interventions always start with a small group.

questions.q: At 90% confidence the intervals are offline $108.11 to $113.46 and online $109.15 to $124.18. They:
options: Cannot be compared at different z values
No longer overlap, so online wins
Overlap only because the SD changed
Still overlap, so the verdict is unchanged
questions.why: Tightening the confidence narrows both intervals but never separates them; at 99% the overlap is larger still.

questions.q: When intervals overlap, the professor's advice on collecting more online data was:
options: Usually unnecessary - the existing data has more to say if you look at it differently, which is Session 4
Reduce the confidence level until they separate
questions.why: Session 4 uses the same 31,634 rows and reaches a conclusion.

questions.q: For the binary variable 9Online, the professor said mean and SD:
options: Do not make much sense - the average just reports the proportion of ones; for many categories use the median
Should be replaced by the mode
questions.why: 12.2% of customers are online is the sensible statement, not "mean 0.122, SD 0.327".

questions.q: Mr Ambani buys a house in your neighbourhood. Should his income be excluded from the locality's average?
options: It depends on the question: keep it when estimating total tax revenue, drop it when asking whether the typical resident is wealthy
questions.why: The same value is an outlier for one question and the whole point for another.

questions.q: Collecting additional data points after seeing the analysis, to fill in what you wish you had observed, is:
options: A shortcut to a biased result - collect first, analyse later
questions.why: Data gathered to match a conclusion cannot test that conclusion.

questions.q: Flagging a credit-card month of several lakh when 90% of months fall between Rs. 22,000 and Rs. 30,000 is:
options: Anomaly detection - a value outside its usual interval triggers an alert
questions.why: The same confidence-interval mathematics pointed at a different question - the one a SOC baseline asks.

questions.q: The professor's closing hint was that, in the Pilgrim data, younger customers are:
options: More likely to be online and more profitable
More likely to be online and less profitable
questions.why: The real file agrees: about 20% of the youngest category is online against under 4% of the oldest, and profit rises with age.

questions.q: In the hint grid, within each age group, online beats offline by:
options: $20 for the young and $50 for the old
questions.why: -$30 vs -$50 for the young; +$350 vs +$300 for the old.

questions.q: Yet the overall column averages in that grid come out as:
The reversal in the grid - online wins in every row but loses overall - is caused by:
options: The two groups having different age mixes, and age driving profit
questions.why: Compare like with like (young with young, old with old) and the true effect reappears - the plan for Session 4.

questions.q: The Excel function that returns the cushion of a 95% interval directly is:
questions.why: It equals 1.96 x SD / SQRT(n); NORM.S.INV(0.975), not 0.95, gives the 1.96.

questions.q: A SOC manager reviews the tickets that analysts remember as difficult to judge quality. This is:
options: Convenience sampling with a bias towards memorable cases
questions.why: Draw tickets at random across customers, severities and shifts instead.

questions.q: The decision to charge a fee or pay a rebate applies to:
options: The population of about five million customers
questions.why: That is why the whole exercise is about inferring the population from the sample.

questions.q: Which statement is consistent with the professor's view of customers?
options: Customers are God and must always be served
Loss-making customers should be refused service
Customers are the means of the company's success, so some are worth keeping, some changing and some letting go
questions.why: The profitability curve makes the idea unavoidable; Section 3.3 shows how it is done without refusing anyone.

questions.q: From the case slides, the standard deviation of profit among profitable customers ($306) against loss-making customers ($45) tells you:
options: Profitable customers vary enormously while losses are small and similar - the number of loss-makers, not any one of them, hurts the bank
questions.why: Average profitable customer $251.45; average loss-maker -$52.19; maximum $2,071; minimum -$221.

questions.q: "The profit of the profitable customers is 21% more than the actual total" and "17% of the good customers' profit goes to loss-makers" are:
options: Two readings of the same numbers: $4,288,303 against $3,527,276, and $761,027 of $4,288,303
questions.why: The peak of the curve is 121.6%; the losses are 17.7% of the gross.

questions.q: The confidence level of an interval is:
options: The probability that the interval contains the real population mean
questions.why: Higher confidence is better; a narrower interval is better; the two pull against each other.

questions.q: According to the case slides, an interval is too wide when:
options: Your decision would differ at its lower limit and at its upper limit
questions.why: If the bank would act the same way at $108.50 and at $114.51, that interval is narrow enough for its question.

questions.q: A hypothesis test always involves:
options: As many statements as there are variables
Two statements about the sample, tested with population data
Two statements about the population, tested with sample data
questions.why: H0 and H1 are claims about the population; the sample is only the evidence.

questions.q: The null and alternate hypotheses must be:
questions.why: They cannot both be true, and one of them must be - together they cover every possibility.

questions.q: On the Delhi Metro, the "sample" the passengers used was:
options: The other passengers in the compartment
A lifetime of observing what usually goes with what
questions.why: Nobody knew the truth; everyone compared what they saw with their experience and found a mismatch.

questions.q: The only two possible outcomes of a hypothesis test are:
options: Reject H0 or do not reject H0
questions.why: Both verdicts are worded around the null.

questions.q: "Do not reject H0" means:
options: The evidence is not strong enough to decide - inconclusive
questions.why: Not rejecting is not accepting; the professor repeated it twice on request.

questions.q: The only hypothesis you can ever accept is:
questions.why: Rejecting H0 is the only conclusive verdict, and it means accepting H1.

questions.q: The rule for framing a hypothesis is:
options: Put whatever you want to establish in the alternate; its negation becomes the null
Put the larger group in the null
Put the status quo in the alternate
Put the action you will take in the null
questions.why: Only "reject H0" is decisive, so the statement you need must be the one that gets accepted.

questions.q: Case 1 for the shampoo (H0: the formula reduces hair fall) is useful to:
options: A competitor or consumer advocacy group that wants to prove the claim false
The FMCG company that wants to advertise
questions.why: Rejecting that null establishes that the formula does not work - their win, not the company's.

questions.q: Under Case 2 (H0: does not reduce; H1: reduces), rejecting H0 lets the company:
options: Advertise, and defend the claim in court with the data
Accept that the formula is no better
questions.why: That is why the company frames it this way: one of the two outcomes lets it act.

questions.q: For Pilgrim Bank, "H0: charge a fee" is a poor hypothesis because:
options: Hypotheses must be about what the data shows (profit), not the action you will take
questions.why: The fact being tested is who is more profitable; fee or rebate is what you do with the verdict.

questions.q: In the Pilgrim hypotheses, the equality sign always appears in:
questions.why: The test begins by assuming the null is true and asking how likely the sample is; "equal" is the natural starting point.

questions.q: Frame A: H0 average offline >= average online. If H0 is rejected, the bank:
questions.why: Rejecting establishes that online customers are more profitable.

questions.q: Frame B: H0 average offline <= average online. If H0 is not rejected, the bank:
options: Offers the rebate as its fallback
questions.why: And that fallback is a calculated hit: costs may rise if online is not really more profitable.

questions.q: The risk of Frame A's fallback (fee when inconclusive) is:
options: Customer pushback from a blanket fee on thin evidence, though no increase in the bank's cost
questions.why: Frame B's fallback risks cost; Frame A's risks customers.

questions.q: Choosing between Frame A and Frame B is:
options: A management decision about which mistake you would rather risk
questions.why: Same data, opposite default actions; the frame encodes the risk appetite.

questions.q: A Type I error is:
questions.why: On the Metro: reporting a mother whose baby really is hers.

questions.q: A Type II error is:
questions.why: On the Metro: doing nothing while a kidnapper walks away.

questions.q: The level of significance, alpha, is:
options: The probability of a Type II error
The tolerance for a Type I error - the maximum probability you accept of rejecting a true null
questions.why: The methodology keeps the Type I probability within alpha; it does not directly control Type II.

questions.q: The most commonly used alpha is:
questions.why: 10% for low-stakes decisions, 1% for high stakes, 0.1% or 0.01% for nuclear plants.

questions.q: A vendor claims its automation will raise your productivity; adopting means redesigning processes and re-staffing. The appropriate alpha is:
options: 10%, to give the vendor a fair chance
1%, because the cost of going wrong is very high
questions.why: You want the pilot to show a significant improvement before committing.

questions.q: The way to reduce the probability of a Type II error is:
questions.why: The test guards Type I; Type II shrinks with sample size.

The null was wrong from the start

questions.q: The p-value is:
options: The probability that H1 is true
The probability of getting a sample like ours if H0 is true
The probability that H0 is true
questions.why: It is about the sample given the null, not about the null given the sample.

questions.q: You reject H0 when:
options: The p-value is greater than alpha
The p-value is less than alpha
The p-value equals the confidence level
questions.why: A sample that would be a near-miracle under H0 is evidence against H0.

questions.q: A p-value of 0.21 with alpha = 0.05 means:
options: Do not reject H0 - a sample like this occurs one time in five under H0
questions.why: Not a miracle, so the null stands unrefuted.
